transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM), Liam (Orchid ML), Priya (Platform Eng), Marco (SRE), Aisha (Product)

Summary:
Quick scoping for POC acceptance boundaries focused on latency vs cost tradeoffs - specifically how we define TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (time-per-output-token) SLOs, how we measure p95/p99, and a practical measurement plan (warm/cold, synthetic vs replay).

Topics:
- Definitions: TTFT vs TPOT and why both matter
- Workload sizing: concurrency, QPS, prompt/response token distributions
- Benchmark types: cold-start, warm steady-state, burst/spike tests, tail-latency focused runs
- Measurement method: tracing, sampling windows, percentile calc and sliding windows
- Acceptance criteria and pass/fail matrix by model variant and deployment mode
- Timeline and responsibilities for lab runs

Action items (also captured in metadata): see action_items list

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick round of intros?
[00:12] Liam (Orchid): Liam O'Connor, Head of ML at Orchid Financial - we're trying to land a POC to validate latency and cost for our chat assistant.
[00:18] Priya (Orchid): Priya, platform eng, I'll be helping with traffic capture and infra.
[00:22] Marco (Orchid): Marco SRE. I'll handle network and test envs.
[00:25] Maya: Great. Jordan and Sofia from my side, Jordan's our solutions engineer and will run the perf lab.
[00:30] Jordan (Redwood SE): Hey all. Focus today is to agree success criteria — how we define TTFT vs TPOT, what p95/p99 targets look like, and what we'll actually run to validate.

[01:05] Aisha (Orchid): Quick background — Benchmarked a couple of clouds internally. Our main concerns: first-response latency for interactive use (chat), and cost per response when we do higher throughput batched inference.

[02:00] Jordan: Right, so we split metric space into two orthogonal SLOs: TTFT = time from request accepted by the infra to first generated token emitted; TPOT = amortized time per additional output token (roughly delta between tokens once streaming begins) — both matter because TTFT affects perceived interactivity and TPOT drives throughput/cost.
[02:22] Liam: We've seen teams only look at avg latency and get surprised by tail spikes. We need p95 and p99 specifically.

[03:05] Maya: Proposal example: for our chat workload, target TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 600ms; TPOT p95 <= 20ms/token, p99 <= 70ms/token for a 512-token response distribution. These numbers are placeholders — want to confirm with your profile.
[03:29] Priya: That p95 250ms seems ambitious for our current infra but plausible on Redwood hosted/dedicated. Can you call out cold starts vs warm?

[04:00] Jordan: Good point — we'll define test buckets: cold-start (model server restarted, empty caches), warm-steady (after 10s of steady traffic to populate KV cache), and warmed-KV (with prefix cache hit rates simulated). Acceptance matrix will be different per bucket — e.g., cold TTFT p95 allowed up to 1.2s, but warm TTFT target is 250ms p95.

[05:10] Liam: Also want to capture variability by prompt length — short (<=32 tokens), medium (~128), and long (~512). Our traffic is ~55% short, 30% medium, 15% long.

[06:00] Jordan: We'll ingest your token histogram and synthesize requests to match that distribution in the lab. We recommend two suites: functional replay (real requests) and synthetic stress (sustained QPS sweeps and 10x spike test).

[07:12] Marco: Network jitter and VPC peering could add noise. We'll need to replicate both a low-latency colocated test and a more realistic cross-region test.

[08:00] Jordan: Measurement plan details:
- Tools: wrk for steady-state QPS, a custom streaming harness for TTFT/TPOT timing, and Jaeger traces for end-to-end.
- Token accounting: we will record input tokens vs output tokens; TPOT will be normalized to output tokens only.
- Percentile calc: sliding 5-minute windows and overall run percentile; p95/p99 computed after removing a 30s warmup period per run.
- Sampling: full sampling for 1 in 1 during lab runs; for longer production runs we'll use 1/10 sampling and reconstruct with counters.

[09:05] Priya: How do you handle batching effects? Our production will have batching at the runtime layer and we'd like to know effective TPOT under different batch sizes.

[09:30] Jordan: We'll run matrix tests across batch sizes (1, 4, 8, 16) and measure both per-request TTFT and amortized TPOT. We'll also report effective cost per output-token based on GPU utilization and token throughput.

[10:20] Liam: For pass/fail, can we have a tiered acceptance: green / amber / red? Green = meets TTFT and TPOT p95/p99 for warm steady-state; amber = marginal but tunable with config changes; red = fails and needs model/deploy changes.

[11:00] Maya: Yup. We'll produce an SLO matrix CSV. Example row: model_variant, deployment_mode (hosted/dedicated/private), bucket (cold/warm), TTFT_p95, TTFT_p99, TPOT_p95, TPOT_p99, notes.

[12:12] Aisha: Important to include cost delta in the decision — e.g., moving from 16-bit quant to 8-bit gives X% latency improvement but Y% degradation in quality and Z% cost reduction.

[13:10] Jordan: We will attach per-run cost estimates using your token distribution and our GPU-cost model. That will let you decide tradeoffs.

[14:05] Priya: Measurement noise: what's your approach to outliers or infra blips?

[14:25] Jordan: We'll flag outliers if they correlate with infra events (CPU steal, OOM, network retries). For raw SLO numbers we'll report both raw percentiles and trimmed percentiles (remove top 0.1% or events tied to infra alerts). But acceptance should be based on trimmed percentiles plus root-cause checks.

[15:30] Marco: On credentials - we'll need a short-lived token and VPC peering. Can you supply a test image for our side?

[15:45] Maya: We'll give you a test account and an ephemeral API key for the lab, plus a link to the test harness repo.

[16:10] Liam: Walk me through a sample test plan and timeline.

[16:30] Jordan: Proposed timeline:
- Day 0-2: data collection — Orchid shares token histograms and 3 prompt sets.
- Day 3-6: baseline runs on Redwood hosted default model, cold and warm.
- Day 7-11: tuning — batch sizes, quantization variants, KV cache config.
- Day 12-14: final acceptance runs + report.
Total ~2 weeks hands-on.

[17:40] Priya: We may need a week contingency for private deployment networking.

[18:05] Maya: We'll build that into the schedule.

[19:00] Aisha: For reporting, show the p95/p99 tables, latency histograms, cost per 1k responses, and config diff.

[20:15] Jordan: Also include sequence-length conditioned percentiles so you can see that long responses drive tail latency.

[21:00] Liam: What about concurrency targets? Our expectation is 40 QPS peak with 200 concurrent open connections (user interactive), and a batch job of 200 QPS for nightly generation.

[21:40] Jordan: We'll validate both patterns. For interactive 40 QPS we'll examine tail latency under 200 concurrent sockets. For batched 200 QPS we'll test throughput and token cost under large batch sizes.

[22:30] Marco: Any security compliance we need to surface before private POC? SAML/SSO, KMS, audit logs?

[22:48] Sofia (CSM): We'll send the SOC2 + encryption/KMS docs. Private POC will require audit log capture; we can enable extended logging in the test account.

[23:30] Priya: Let's talk pass thresholds again — can you share rationale for the p95/p99 numbers?

[23:45] Jordan: Benchmarks we've seen for similar fin/health chat apps: interactive thresholds are tight; human-perceived latency around 200-300ms TTFT feels instant. p99 is allowed more slack. TPOT numbers come from per-token generation kernel latency; e.g., 20ms/token p95 gives ~400ms for 20-token output beyond the first token. We'll model end-to-end perceived latency by TTFT + first N*TPOT for typical N.

[24:50] Liam: Also need to validate quality regressions when moving to more aggressive quantization that reduces latency. Can we pair automated evals?

[25:10] Maya: We'll run a small eval harness with your golden prompts and look for regression alerts. If quality delta exceeds threshold we'll mark performance gains as unacceptable.

[26:00] Aisha: For measurement, what about token-level streaming variability? Some models emit first token slower but subsequent tokens faster.

[26:20] Jordan: That's the exact reason we keep both metrics. TTFT catches the initial cost of scheduling, kernel load, kv lookup; TPOT captures steady-state generation speed. Both are needed to understand interactive feel vs throughput economics.

[27:05] Priya: For sliding windows and percentile stability, is 5-minute window OK?

[27:20] Jordan: 5-minute gives a balance; for fine-grained diagnosis we'll also provide 1-minute windows. Acceptance will use aggregated run-level percentiles after warmup to minimize transient noise.

[28:00] Liam: On tooling, can you share the wrk scripts and streaming harness?

[28:10] Maya: Yes — we'll push the repo link after the call. Jordan will own the harness.

[29:00] Jordan: Anything else on metrics? We'll also log CPU/GPU utilization, batch sizes, queue depths, and queuing delay so we can attribute tail latency.

[30:00] Marco: We'll run one cross-region test to see network effects.

[30:30] Jordan: We'll set a baseline and then run the cross-region. Expect the network to add ~20-60ms depending on region.

[31:00] Aisha: For the amber tier, do we require remediation items to be tracked?

[31:15] Maya: Yes, amber results will come with a recommended tuning run (batching/kv/config) and an estimated lift. We'll retest after tuning.

[32:00] Priya: Can you formalize the acceptance matrix with clear pass criteria so procurement can sign off?

[32:15] Maya: We'll provide a CSV SLO matrix and an executive one-page with green/amber/red definitions.

[33:00] Liam: Let's confirm data handling for replay: will Redwood store our prompts during the POC?

[33:20] Sofia: For hosted POC we keep logs for the duration of the test and can enable auto-purge; for private we don't retain inputs. We'll document retention and can enable KMS.

[34:00] Marco: Network and keys: we'll accept short-lived keys.

[34:10] Maya: Noted.

[35:00] Jordan: One more nuance — TPOT is sometimes nonlinear with longer sequences due to KV cache scaling and attention cost; we'll present sequence-conditioned TPOT curves.

[35:50] Priya: Good. On the timeline, can we target the week of Mar 30 for lab runs?

[36:05] Maya: Yes, Jordan will schedule.

[36:30] Liam: If we go to dedicated or private, how much will the SLOs shift?

[36:45] Jordan: Dedicated tends to tighten tail latency — fewer noisy neighbors, predictable batch behavior. Private can be similar but depends on your HW. We'll call out delta in the report.

[37:30] Aisha: For reporting, can we have an itemized cost-to-improve chart so we can evaluate tradeoffs?

[37:40] Jordan: Yes — cost per 1k responses across variants and configs.

[38:10] Priya: Regarding SLO windows — how long should acceptance be observed? One-off runs can be flaky.

[38:25] Jordan: We prefer multiple runs over different days — at least three stable runs for acceptance. For production rollout we can set a 7-day rolling window for SLO monitoring.

[39:10] Marco: Anything around retries/failed streams?

[39:25] Jordan: We'll instrument retries and count them separately. SLOs will exclude successful retried requests but report retry rate as a separate metric; if retry rate > threshold it affects acceptance.

[40:00] Liam: For TPOT reporting, do you normalize for output token length?

[40:10] Jordan: TPOT is per-output-token by definition; we will normalize and also provide total response time distributions for each length bucket.

[41:00] Aisha: Who signs off on final acceptance?

[41:10] Maya: We'll send a sign-off doc. Typically your Head of ML + Platform (Liam + Priya) sign off after reviewing the final report; Redwood PM signs off on lab completion.

[41:40] Liam: Ok. Anything else?

[41:50] Priya: One ask — show both shaded ranges for p95 and p99 in reports so stakeholders can quickly see variance.

[42:10] Jordan: We'll include histograms and shaded percentile bands.

[43:00] Sofia: I'll follow up with SOC2 and retention docs and a short checklist for private POC prep.

[43:15] Maya: Recap of next steps: Maya sends SLO template + repo link; Liam shares token histograms; Jordan schedules lab and prepares harness; Marco sets up peering/keys; run during week of 30th.

[44:00] Liam: Sounds good.

[44:10] Aisha: Thanks everyone.

[44:20] Maya: Thanks — we’ll email the plan and the action items.

[44:30] (end)
